Characters missing both arms means or perform any tasks requiring manual dexterity without magic, tools or other remarkable means approved by the Storyteller. Characters missing a leg can move at a crutch or peg leg and are at -3 on Athletics rolls involving footwork. Those with a paralyzed leg must also use crutches or drag the paralyzed limb behind them, suffering the same penalties as true amputees. Quadriplegics may not attempt most physical tasks. Such tortured invalids seldom live long in the harsh Age of Sorrows and make poor concepts for the vast majority of players' characters. At best, they may drag themselves painfully and slowly across the ground with their arms. The value of this Flaw is two points for lack of a single arm, three points for a single missing arm or both hands, five points for the loss of any two limbs, seven points for missing eight points for quadriplegics. Fair or not, the gods do not normally make cripples of the Chosen. As with all major physical deformities, Exalted characters receive less compensation for amputation, gaining one less point for losing a single hand or limb and two less points for amputations involving two or more limbs.
compatibility: Any character type, including Alchemicals; the reduced cost applies to 'Exalted' generically, and Alchemicals are Exalted, so this discount applies to them.
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Players Guide's universal Chapter One, "Merits and Flaws" (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json). JUDGMENT CALL: derived from the Players Guide's universal Chapter One (p. 31/PDF 32). For an Alchemical, a missing limb represents damage that has not yet been repaired at a Vat Complex (see vats-background) rather than a permanent congenital condition, since Refitting can ordinarily replace lost material; this Flaw should be read as reflecting a character who -- for story reasons -- currently lacks access to that repair.

name: Dying
summary: A curse or other fatal condition that will assuredly destroy the character without powerful curative magic. For an Alchemical, this represents an irreversible structural or Essence-flow failure (spreading corrosion, a fracturing soulgem lattice, a runaway Clarity/Dissonance spiral) rather than biological illness; the character loses a dot of Stamina per interval (scaling from years down to days as the Flaw's value rises), reaching destruction at Stamina 0.
mechanics: A character with this Flaw suffers from a curse, a terminal illness or other fatal condition and will assuredly perish without the aid of powerful curative magic. The character loses one dot of Stamina per interval, the length of the interval determined by the value of the Flaw. At the lowest level, this period shortens to months for six points and days for ten points. Once a character reaches Stamina 0, he dies. It is always possible to avert this process by some means before returning to full heroic effort, but not without truly heroic effort. This Flaw aids in depicting heroes who strive bravely against all odds or stories rooted in the quest for a cure. Storytellers should feel free to disallow this Flaw without an appropriate story explanation, especially for Exalted characters or a short game.
compatibility: Any character type, including Alchemicals, with an adaptation: since Alchemicals are immune to ordinary disease and do not age or sicken biologically, this Flaw for an Alchemical represents a slow, incurable structural or Essence-flow failure (a spreading material corrosion, a fracturing soulgem lattice, or a runaway Clarity/Dissonance spiral) rather than a biological terminal illness.
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Players Guide's universal Chapter One, "Merits and Flaws" (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json). JUDGMENT CALL, FLAGGED: derived from the Players Guide's universal Chapter One (pp. 31-32/PDF 32-33). The source's own framing (curse, terminal illness, fatal condition) does not translate directly to a construct; reframed around a fatal Essence/structural degradation while keeping the underlying mechanic (losing a dot of Stamina per interval, dying at Stamina 0) unchanged. The source's own caution that Storytellers should be more willing to disallow this Flaw for Exalted characters applies with extra force here.

name: Small
summary: Stands only four and a half feet tall or less, with a reduced effective Strength for weapon/tool size requirements and one fewer -1 health level. For an Alchemical, this represents an unusually small vat-built chassis within her current Essence-tier size range, distinct from the separate size growth that comes from raising Essence itself.
mechanics: A character with this Flaw stands only four and a half feet tall or less. She has difficulty reaching and manipulating objects designed for normal adult size, reducing her effective Strength by one dot for the sole purpose of meeting the minimum requirements of weapons and large tools. Her reduced size also costs her one -1 health level. Lunar Exalted with this Flaw appear proportionally smaller in all forms unless assuming a specific guise as with Prey's Skin Disguise (see E:tL, p. 129). In addition to representing children or short adults or pygmy races such as the Djala, this Flaw can aid in portraying extremely gaunt and frail characters of normal height (especially in conjunction with low Stamina).
compatibility: Any character type, including Alchemicals. The source's Lunar-specific clause (size reduction carrying into every form via Prey's Skin Disguise) does not apply, since Alchemicals do not shapechange; an Alchemical's overall size is instead governed by her own Essence-linked growth (see alchemical-refitting-essence-and-evolution), and this Flaw represents an unusually small vat-built chassis within that framework.
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Players Guide's universal Chapter One, "Merits and Flaws" (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json). JUDGMENT CALL: mirrors the Large Size Merit's adaptation above. Derived from the Players Guide's universal Chapter One (p. 32/PDF 33).

name: Disfigured
summary: Wretched physical deformity, from concealable scarring/pitting (3-pt., Appearance capped at 1) to monstrous full-body horror (4-pt., Appearance 0, automatic social revulsion). For an Alchemical, this is reframed as visibly scarred, mismatched, or crudely-repaired chassis material (exposed wiring, a cracked faceplate, non-matching salvaged Magical Material) rather than the source's Lunar-Tell/Abyssal-rot examples.
mechanics: Characters with this Flaw suffer some wretched deformity. For three points, they might bear the pitted pockmarks of a smallpox survivor, gross birth defects, heavy scarring from burns or wounds, useless protrusions of Wyld-warped flesh or something stranger still. Exalted and other magical beings may suffer deformities appropriate to their nature, such as a Lunar with a hideous Tell or ghosts with excessively prominent death marks. Characters with the lowest version of the Flaw cannot ever have an Appearance rating greater than 1 and lose one die from other Social pools in which their unsightly deformity could prove a hindrance. It is usually possible to conceal three-point deformities with heavy clothes, masks or other garb. While so attired, the character suffers no penalty and may act as though he has a normal Appearance unless the other party knows his true visage. Characters with Appearance 1 who do not have this Flaw are simply ugly, but not strikingly so. The four-point version of this Flaw represents truly monstrous deformity: full-body scarring, the gaping pits and rotting abscesses of a leper, hideous Wyld-mutation or something even more horrible still. Wretches at this level of hideousness have an Appearance of 0 that cannot be improved with bonus or experience points and automatically fail any Appearance-based roll. All but the most tolerant and charitable souls (Compassion 4+) will respond to the character with utter revulsion and disgust, resulting in a two-die penalty on most Social rolls. At best, monstrous characters can expect contempt and pity. In crueler regions, they may be run out of town or stoned for public amusement. Abyssal Exalted may take this Flaw with Storyteller approval to represent a rotted or death-twisted visage. Storytellers may certainly default to the rules as written in E:Ab, giving no bonus-point reward to players who choose the path of decay and putrescence. However, the game effects of this Flaw adequately represent the fear and loathing a rotted Abyssal will engender in most people.
compatibility: Any character type, including Alchemicals; the source's own worked example ('a Lunar with a hideous Tell') does not apply, but the underlying concept (a visible, Exalt-appropriate deformity) reframes cleanly as scarred, mismatched, or crudely-repaired chassis material -- exposed wiring, a cracked faceplate, or a patchwork of non-matching Magical Material.
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Players Guide's universal Chapter One, "Merits and Flaws" (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json). JUDGMENT CALL: derived from the Players Guide's universal Chapter One (pp. 32-33/PDF 33-34). Dropped the source's Lunar Tell and Abyssal-rotted-visage examples as inapplicable, substituting an Alchemical-appropriate chassis-damage framing while keeping the mechanical effects (Appearance cap, Social penalties) unchanged.

name: Slow Healing
summary: Mortals with this Flaw heal at half the normal rate; Exalted with this Flaw instead recover at the normal MORTAL rate (rather than their usual superhuman rate), though they still heal perfectly from anything short of amputation given time.
mechanics: Mortal characters with this Flaw recover from injury at half their normal rate. Most such characters do not live long in the brutal Age of Sorrows. Exalted with this Flaw instead recover from their wounds at the rate of normal mortals, but given sufficient time, they still heal perfectly from anything less than amputation.
compatibility: Any character type, including Alchemicals; Exalted (including Alchemicals) get the milder, mortal-rate healing variant rather than the harsher half-mortal rate mortals suffer.
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Players Guide's universal Chapter One, "Merits and Flaws" (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json). Derived from the Players Guide's universal Chapter One (p. 33/PDF 34). Interacts with this family's own alchemical-life-and-death row, which otherwise has a fed Alchemical healing exactly like other Exalted.

name: Weak Immune System
summary: Harder time fighting off illness; mortals add 2 to Endurance/Resistance difficulty vs. disease/infection, while Exalted instead halve their relevant dice pools but keep their usual immunity to the ailment's actual mechanical effects (discomfort only).
mechanics: Mortal characters with this Flaw have a harder time fighting off illness, their players adding 2 to the difficulty of all Endurance and Resistance rolls for the characters to resist disease and infection. Exalted characters instead half their dice pools to resist or throw off such maladies (rounded down) but retain their usual superhuman resilience to the actual effects of ailments they contract. This means that Chosen with this Flaw will experience the discomfort and distraction of illness for long bouts at a time, perhaps making them wish they were dead even if they are never in any real danger.
compatibility: Any character type, including Alchemicals; Exalted (including Alchemicals) pay the reduced 3-pt. cost and get the milder mechanical variant (halved dice pool, but no loss of usual immunity to an ailment's real effects).
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Players Guide's universal Chapter One, "Merits and Flaws" (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json). JUDGMENT CALL: derived from the Players Guide's universal Chapter One (p. 33/PDF 34). Cross-checked against alchemical-artificial-metabolism, which already grants Alchemicals blanket immunity to non-magical disease/infection; this Flaw remains meaningful for an Alchemical's resistance to poison and magical disease, which that row does not cover, mirroring the same partial-overlap reasoning as the Special Resistance Merit above.

name: Diminished Attributes
summary: Weaker, slower, less healthy (or, in the Mental/Social variants, less bright/uncouth) bodies than normal adults; grants three points per Physical Attribute dot forfeited during character creation (cannot forfeit the free dot in each Attribute, and cannot be bought back with bonus points).
mechanics: Characters with this Flaw have weaker, slower or less healthy bodies than normal adults. This may be atrophy induced by old age, injury or illness, or perhaps the character is a child who has not developed into full maturity. Regardless, the character receives three points for every Physical Attribute dot forfeited during character creation. Characters cannot use this Flaw to forfeit the free dot they receive in each Attribute, and obviously, may not spend bonus points to purchase Physical Attributes. Alternate versions of this Flaw apply to Mental and Social Attributes for characters who are less bright or particularly uncouth. Note that these are considered Mental and Social Flaws rather than falling into the Physical category.
compatibility: Any character type, including Alchemicals; no splat-specific variant is given.
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Players Guide's universal Chapter One, "Merits and Flaws" (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json). Derived from the Players Guide's universal Chapter One (p. 33/PDF 34). Applies to any of an Alchemical's nine Attributes exactly as for other Exalted.

name: Diminished Sense
summary: Partial or total loss of a sense; total loss is normally worth three bonus points (two for senses other than sight/hearing), reduced by one if the character has access to a compensating device. Exalted receive one less bonus point per Diminished Sense and may not have more than one sense loss in total.
mechanics: The character suffers partial or total loss of a sense. In the case of partial loss, this Flaw adds 1 to the difficulty of all Awareness rolls based on the dulled sense. This difficulty increase also applies to other rolls determined by the Storyteller, such as Social rolls in a noisy party for hearing loss or long range attacks for vision. Partial loss of a sense is normally worth three bonus points for hearing or vision and two points for other senses. Reduce this value by one if the character has ready access to magic or a device that compensates or corrects for this loss. Glass or crystal spectacles are not unknown in the Realm and the largest cities of the Threshold, although they are often prohibitively expensive (Resources 4 in the Threshold or the rural Realm, Resources 3 in Nexus, the Imperial City or other metropoli, Resources 2 in Chiaroscuro). Total loss of a sense ensures that a character automatically fails any rolls exclusively dependent on that sense, especially Awareness. This loss also adds anywhere from 1 to 3 to the base difficulty of rolls requiring a conjunction of the missing sense and other senses. The Storyteller will impose other penalties as appropriate: Blind characters cannot attack targets beyond 100 yards without magic or an extraordinary stunt and subtract two successes from all attacks and other actions dependent on sight. Deafness makes speech more difficult and requires a Perception + Linguistics roll (difficulty 3+) to lip-read others, making some sort of shared sign language useful. Numbness prevents most pain (halving wound penalties), but the character also cannot discern temperature, feel pleasure or know when she is suffering injury. The value of this Flaw is six points for blindness, four for deafness or numbness and three for loss of smell and taste. The Storyteller may adjust these costs as needed for characters who find ways to circumvent a lost sense or find the loss even more debilitating for some reason. Exalted characters receive one less bonus point per sense for any Diminished Sense, as the gods are loathe to choose people with serious handicaps. No Exalt may have more than one sense loss in its entirety.
compatibility: Any character type, including Alchemicals; Exalted (including Alchemicals) receive one less bonus point per sense and may not stack more than one Diminished Sense.
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Players Guide's universal Chapter One, "Merits and Flaws" (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json). Derived from the Players Guide's universal Chapter One (p. 33/PDF 34).

name: Derangement
summary: The curse of madness, drawing from the Exalted core rulebook's derangement list (p. 281) or the book's own suggested forms (Depression, Glossolalia, Hysteria, Sadism); suppressible for a scene with a Willpower point but only curable by magic or lengthy counseling.
mechanics: A character with this Flaw suffers the curse of madness. Perhaps he dallied too close to the warping energies of the Wyld or angered a wrathful spirit or maybe there is no obvious or overt cause. Regardless, his mind suffers regular debilitating bouts of its infirmity. Characters with this Flaw have one of the derangements listed on page 281 of Exalted. It is also possible to suppress the worst effects of this derangement for a scene for a cost of one Willpower point. However, it requires magic or lengthy counseling to actually cure a derangement. The actual game effects of madness are left to your imagination, but the character will probably lose at least two dice from most Social pools with characters who do not share the madness. Characters receive three points for their first derangement and only one point for each subsequent form of madness. Other possible derangements include: Depression (observing or experiencing pain or emotional distress overwhelms the character, causing him to act as though suffering from the Virtue Flaw Heart of Tears, see Exalted, p. 131); Glossolalia (under stress, the character begins speaking loudly in tongues for the rest of the scene; only powerful magic can interpret the meaning of such verbal outbursts, assuming they have any coherence; this derangement primarily manifests in true prophets, shamans and characters with the Whispers Background); Hysteria (under stress, the character lashes out in blind rage as though suffering from the Virtue Flaw Berserk Anger, see Exalted, p. 133); Sadism (with only minor provocation, the character behaves as if constantly suffering from the Virtue Flaw Deliberate Cruelty, see Exalted, p. 132; this also has an effective Compassion rating of 1 until and unless the madness passes, regardless of her true rating).
compatibility: Any character type, including Alchemicals; no splat-specific variant is given.
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Players Guide's universal Chapter One, "Merits and Flaws" (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json). Derived from the Players Guide's universal Chapter One (pp. 33-34/PDF 34-35). Cross-checked against Alchemical's own Clarity Trait (clarity-trait): Derangement is a distinct, universal mental-flaw mechanic layered on top of Clarity/Dissonance, not a substitute for either.

name: Amnesia
summary: Large gaps in the character's memory, from a single missing life event (1 pt.) up to recurring amnesia that prevents remembering anything prior to the last sleep (5 pts.). The source's additional Celestial-Exalted-only 1-pt. option (remembering nothing of previous incarnations) does not apply to Alchemicals, who have no reincarnation cycle.
mechanics: Characters with this Flaw suffer large gaps in memory. For one point, the character is missing a notable section of his life (such as childhood) or cannot remember a very crucial event (Exaltation, committing an atrocity). Celestial Exalted who remember absolutely nothing from any previous incarnations of their Exaltation may also purchase Amnesia for one point. For two points, the character remembers nothing from a vast swath of her life: everything before Exaltation, decades spent as a death cultist, etc. For five points, the amnesia is recurring and prevents the character from remembering anything prior to waking up from her last sleep. The character still preserves memory, but cannot access it. Such characters may retain fragmentary memories from before they received the injury or psychic trauma that damaged their mind. Additionally, recurring amnesia prevents characters from learning or advancing Abilities unless they can somehow keep themselves awake or keep a thorough journal. Characters with any version of Amnesia have all their Traits and capabilities, although they often do not know what they can do and certainly do not remember how and when they learned. Likewise, they may find forgotten friends and enemies faintly familiar but may mistake friend for foe and vice versa if the Storyteller feels particularly cruel. Players of amnesiacs should consider letting the Storyteller spend most or all of the character's bonus points to create actual surprises, but this obviously requires a deep level of trust. As an optional rule to encourage suspenseful play, any 'hidden' Traits cost one less bonus point each, but these only emerge when the Storyteller sees fit to reveal them.
compatibility: Any character type, including Alchemicals, at the general 1/2/5-pt. mortal-facing scale. The source's additional 1-pt. option for Celestial Exalted (Solar/Lunar/Sidereal) who remember nothing of prior incarnations does not apply to Alchemicals, who do not reincarnate the way Celestial Exalted do.
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Players Guide's universal Chapter One, "Merits and Flaws" (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json). JUDGMENT CALL: derived from the Players Guide's universal Chapter One (p. 34/PDF 35). Dropped the Celestial-Exalted-specific past-incarnation clause as inapplicable; the general memory-loss framing (missing childhood, missing pre-Exaltation life, recurring amnesia) still applies cleanly to an Alchemical.

name: Superstition
summary: A wrong or fanatical idea about something important, treated by the character as sincere fact; scales from a simple personal inconvenience (1 pt.) to a belief that seriously harms others if acted upon (3 pts.).
mechanics: Creation is a magical world where physical laws often a matter of divine whim or are torn asunder by the encroachment of the Wyld or shadowlands. Strange local beliefs and customs are very often real and meaningful -- and perhaps even necessary. Unfortunately, characters with this Flaw hold a wrong or fanatical idea about something important. Perhaps this erroneous belief was once rooted in fact or a kernel of truth, but that time is long past. The value of this Flaw depends on the deviation and danger of the character's superstitious beliefs. For one point, the custom is simply inconvenient. The character might believe that road spirits abhor travelers who walk in a straight line down their path or that a certain livestock animal is inherently unclean and therefore unsuitable for human consumption. At two points, the superstition is actually dangerous to oneself (or to others who believe it). The character may think that garlic repels the undead or put faith in a medicine that does nothing against harm. Three-point versions of this Flaw involve harm to others. Characters may seriously believe the year will not return from the chaos of Calibration unless they receive a dedicated sacrifice of a virgin, or they may believe that anyone who commits adultery must die by public stoning. Exercise of such beliefs they are not the law of the land may get a character in trouble with the authorities or incur retaliation. Characters who discover and come to accept the falsehood of their superstitions must buy off this Flaw for experience. Characters receive one less point for this Flaw if the game will take place mostly in areas where the belief is commonly held.
compatibility: Any character type, including Alchemicals; no splat-specific variant is given.
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Players Guide's universal Chapter One, "Merits and Flaws" (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json). Derived from the Players Guide's universal Chapter One (p. 34/PDF 35). Autochthonia's own Theomachracy and Sodality cultures provide ready in-setting analogues to the source's Creation-flavored superstition examples.

name: Vice
summary: A moral weakness, sin, or failing that tempts the character above all others (e.g. bigotry, carnal cruelty, secret cowardice); when relevant, the character loses two dice from the affected Virtue for every point invested and may indulge in it over better judgment. This Flaw may not alter or ameliorate Clarity, the Alchemical analog to the source's Great Curse cross-reference.
mechanics: A character with this Flaw suffers a particular sin or failing that tempts him above all others. A warrior of great Valor may harbor a secret fear of the undead. A monk who masters ascetic Temperance may yet fall to the lure of carnal desire. Those of great Conviction may find their implacable confidence shattered when they must assume a position of leadership. Deep Compassion may mask a streak of bigotry and cruelty toward a group of people or an utter disinterest in romance. In situations relevant to the sinful condition, the character loses two dice from the affected Virtue for every point invested in the Vice. This may reduce the dice pool of a Virtue to zero, in which case the character automatically indulges in the sin and immoderation of his Vice over the better judgment of his morality. Characters may not have more than one Vice. Instead, those with deep moral deficiencies are Callous (see p. 35). This Flaw may not alter or ameliorate the Great Curse, and Storytellers should ban any Vice that obviously attempts to circumvent this restriction.
compatibility: Any character type, including Alchemicals; the source's Great Curse cross-reference (Solar/Lunar's Limit-Trait analog) is replaced for Alchemicals by their own Clarity Trait, since this family has no Great Curse (see clarity-trait). This Flaw may not alter or ameliorate Clarity.
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Players Guide's universal Chapter One, "Merits and Flaws" (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json). ADAPTED CROSS-REFERENCE: derived from the Players Guide's universal Chapter One (p. 34/PDF 35). Alchemicals have no Great Curse or Limit Trait; their equivalent signature Trait is Clarity (clarity-trait), so this row's restriction is retargeted at Clarity rather than at the Great Curse, preserving the source's intent (this Flaw cannot be used to weaken or bypass the splat's own core corruption/Limit-analog mechanic).

name: Addiction
summary: An addiction to some substance, scaling 1-3 points by legality/danger/expense, +1 if the character's standing wealth can't support the habit, +2 if it consumes the character's entire life. Exalted (including Alchemicals) subtract one from the addiction's rating owing to hardier constitutions. The source's Wyld-addiction variant (cross-referenced to Exalted: The Lunars) is dropped as inapplicable; substitute an Autochthonia-appropriate substance instead.
mechanics: Characters with this Flaw suffer an addiction to some substance, without which they suffer the discomfort -- and perhaps danger -- of withdrawal. For one point, this substance is relatively easy and legal to obtain, inexpensive enough that the habit will not bankrupt the character and reasonably safe barring excessive overdose. Examples include alcohol, qat and marijuana. For two points, the substance is more serious due to rarity or more debilitating side effects. Examples include opium, rasp spider venom and ice fern spores. Three-point addictions are expensive and/or dangerous, such as rock cocaine, heroin and bright morning. Addiction to the Wyld also awards three points. Add one to the value of an addiction if the character's Resources cannot support regular use. Add two if the character cannot possibly afford a single dose and must turn to theft or deep debt or if the addiction controls the character's entire life. Exalted subtract one from the rating of their addictions, owing to their hardier constitutions. Actual effects of addiction and withdrawal depend on the drug and Storyteller discretion but may include dice penalties, damage or rolls to remain conscious. Thorough information on the drug trade and most of the example drugs can be found in Chapter Two of Manacle and Coin. Rules for Wyld addiction may be found on page 205 of E:tL.
compatibility: Any character type, including Alchemicals; Exalted (including Alchemicals) subtract one from their addiction's rating owing to hardier constitutions.
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Players Guide's universal Chapter One, "Merits and Flaws" (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json). JUDGMENT CALL: derived from the Players Guide's universal Chapter One (p. 35/PDF 36). Dropped the source's direct cross-reference to Exalted: The Lunars p. 205 for Wyld addiction rules, since Alchemicals rarely encounter the Wyld directly from within Autochthonia; the general addiction framework (1-5 pt. scale by substance danger/legality/expense) still applies to Autochthonia-appropriate substances (industrial reagents, refined Essence tinctures, etc.) at Storyteller discretion.

name: Callous
summary: Selfish pragmatism over scruples and integrity; gains two bonus points per point of Virtue forfeited during character creation, cannot start with a Willpower rating more than one point higher than the sum of the two highest Virtues, and cannot have the Paragon Nature.
mechanics: A character with this Flaw believes in selfish pragmatism over scruples and integrity. He gains two bonus points for every dot of Virtues his player forfeits during character creation. Callous characters cannot forfeit their last dot of a Virtue and may not begin play with a Willpower rating more than one point higher than the sum of their two highest Virtues. This limit applies until such a time as the character has a total of 9 dots of Virtues, at which point the character automatically loses this Flaw at no cost. Thus, a monstrous, intemperate, inconstant coward with a rating of 1 in all Virtues could never have a Willpower higher than 3. Characters with this Flaw may not have the Paragon Nature. Exalted with this Flaw suffer Virtue Flaws appropriate to their highest Virtue, if applicable.
compatibility: Any character type, including Alchemicals; Exalted (including Alchemicals) with this Flaw suffer the standard Exalted Virtue Flaw tied to their highest Virtue, and may not have the Paragon Nature while this Flaw is active.
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Players Guide's universal Chapter One, "Merits and Flaws" (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json). Derived from the Players Guide's universal Chapter One (p. 35/PDF 36). Cross-references True Paragon (mutually exclusive with this Flaw, exactly as for other splats).

name: Nightmares
summary: Horrific dreams whenever the character sleeps, adding 1 to the difficulty of regaining Willpower via Conviction after sleep, and inflicting lingering one-die penalties and unsoakable bashing damage on a botched Conviction roll. Ghosts apply this penalty to Slumber healing instead.
mechanics: A character with this Flaw experiences horrific dreams whenever she sleeps. She may have experienced a mind-shattering personal trauma or received the attention of malefic spirits or sorcerers, or perhaps she harbors guilt over past misdeeds. Regardless, she finds little solace in slumber and adds 1 to the difficulty to regain Willpower with Conviction after sleep. If the Conviction roll botches, the character loses one point of temporary Willpower and is plagued with lingering horror for the rest of the day, resulting in a one-die penalty to all non-reflexive actions. Ghosts with this Flaw instead apply the difficulty increase to their Stamina roll to heal in Slumber. Failure inflicts an additional level of unsoakable bashing damage, while a botch results in damage and the added die penalty for lingering horror as described above.
compatibility: Any character type, including Alchemicals; the source names only ghosts for a distinct mechanical variant, so Alchemicals use the standard Willpower-regain-based version.
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Players Guide's universal Chapter One, "Merits and Flaws" (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json). JUDGMENT CALL: derived from the Players Guide's universal Chapter One (pp. 35-36/PDF 36-37). Nothing in Alchemical's own rules establishes that Alchemicals do not sleep or dream (see the identical caveat on Prescient Dreamer above); kept as written rather than reframed.

name: Pacifist
summary: Cannot bring himself to fight, adding 1 to the difficulty of attacks (3-pt.), or cannot attack anyone at all without spending a Willpower point to overcome his aversion for a scene (5-pt.).
mechanics: However noble in intent, pacifism carries great risks in the violent, imperfect reality of the Age of Sorrows. Those who will not fight must find protectors who will or suffer at the hands of those less idealistically principled. For three points, a pacifist adds 1 to the difficulty of her attacks. Even retaliation or combat in self-defense carries this penalty, as the character's peaceful nature rebels against the very notion of inflicting harm. Characters with the five-point version of this Flaw may not attack anyone without the expenditure of a Willpower point to overcome her aversion to violence for a scene. Even if they do take violent action out of necessity, such characters add 1 to the difficulty of their attacks.
compatibility: Any character type, including Alchemicals; no splat-specific variant is given.
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Players Guide's universal Chapter One, "Merits and Flaws" (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json). Derived from the Players Guide's universal Chapter One (p. 36/PDF 37).

name: Unskilled
summary: Less education and training than most adults, from youth, dementia, or lack of practice; grants one bonus point per Ability dot forfeited during character creation, though known Favored Abilities must still meet minimum statistical requirements (one dot for Exalted).
mechanics: Characters with this Flaw have less education and training to draw upon than most adults. They may be too young to know much yet or so old that dementia and lack of practice has robbed them of their skill. Perhaps he slept through school, or maybe they just aren't the sharpest knives in the drawer (reflected by low Intelligence or Wits). Whatever the reason, such a character receives one bonus point for every dot of Abilities forfeited during character creation. Characters with this Flaw must still meet the statistic requirements of all known Favored Abilities (one dot for Exalted; all Favored Abilities must equal or above non-Favored for mortals) and obviously cannot purchase Ability dots with bonus points.
compatibility: Any character type, including Alchemicals, with an adaptation: the source's Exalted-specific requirement (must keep at least one dot in any known Favored Ability) does not apply to Alchemicals, who have no Favored Abilities at all (per alchemical-character-creation-overview, all 23 starting Ability dots are freely distributed with no Caste/Favored discount); an Alchemical with this Flaw is otherwise unconstrained in which Ability dots she forfeits.
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Players Guide's universal Chapter One, "Merits and Flaws" (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json). JUDGMENT CALL: derived from the Players Guide's universal Chapter One (p. 36/PDF 37). Alchemicals are the one Exalt type with no Favored Abilities whatsoever, so the generic Exalted floor this Flaw imposes elsewhere simply has no target for Alchemicals; treated as an inapplicable clause rather than a reason to exclude the whole Flaw.

name: Weak-Willed
summary: Gnawing self-doubt and lack of drive; grants one bonus point per dot of permanent Willpower forfeited during character creation, extremely uncommon among the Chosen. Exalted with this Flaw may not begin with Willpower lower than 4 unless also Callous, in which case (or if UnExalted) Willpower can be as low as 2.
mechanics: A character with this Flaw suffers gnawing self-doubt and lack of drive. She may have experienced the hunger of a Fair One or had her mind shattered by wicked sorcery. Or maybe she's simply a pathetic wretch. Regardless, the character gains one bonus point for every dot of permanent Willpower her player forfeits during character creation. This Flaw is extremely uncommon among the Chosen, as the Celestines do not Exalt spiritual weaklings. Only Exalted who suffered Willpower loss since their Exaltation may take this Flaw and only with a remarkable story explanation. Exalted characters with this Flaw may not begin with a Willpower rating lower than 4, unless they are also Callous (see p. 35). UnExalted and Callous Exalted characters may have a Willpower score as low as 2.
compatibility: Any character type, including Alchemicals; Exalted (including Alchemicals) face a floor of Willpower 4 for this Flaw unless also Callous (floor of 2), and it is explicitly stated to be extremely rare for any Exalt to take (requiring a story reason for post-Exaltation Willpower loss).
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Players Guide's universal Chapter One, "Merits and Flaws" (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json). Derived from the Players Guide's universal Chapter One (pp. 36-37/PDF 37-38).

name: Barbarian
summary: Grew up outside the bounds of civilization and does not know the ways of soft city-dwellers; loses one die from all Social dice pools related to understanding or expressing civilized etiquette, and is not assumed literate unless Lore 2+.
mechanics: Characters with this Flaw grew up outside the bounds of civilization and do not know the ways of soft city-dwellers. Such individuals lose one die from all Social dice pools related to understanding or expressing civilized etiquette and are not assumed to be literate unless they have Lore 2 or more. Players playing a barbarian-only game may not take this Flaw unless they interact with civilization on a fairly regular basis in a capacity that makes their upbringing a liability.
compatibility: Any character type, including Alchemicals, with an adaptation: 'civilization' for an Alchemical is Autochthonian Tripartite society (the Olgotary/Theomachracy/Sodalities) rather than Creation's cities; a character raised in an exile colony, the Reaches, or otherwise outside mainstream Autochthonian society could take this Flaw for unfamiliarity with Tripartite etiquette instead of Realm/Threshold etiquette.
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Players Guide's universal Chapter One, "Merits and Flaws" (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json). JUDGMENT CALL: derived from the Players Guide's universal Chapter One (p. 37/PDF 38). Retargeted 'civilization' from Creation's city-states to Autochthonia's own Tripartite society, consistent with backing-background-altered's description of exile-colony and illicit Backing as existing outside that society.

name: Secrets
summary: The character harbors a secret that could prove embarrassing or dangerous if others learn of it, scaling from mild embarrassment (1 pt.) up to deadly, death-penalty-worthy crimes/heresies (3 pts.).
mechanics: The character harbors a secret that could prove embarrassing or even dangerous if others were to learn of it. The value of this Flaw depends on the severity of the affair. For one point, it is something highly inconvenient or humiliating, like a bastard child from an illicit affair. The character's reputation and relationships may suffer, but no harm will befall him if word gets out. For two points, the secret is more serious and will certainly lead to reprisal if it comes to light. Criminals who have gotten away with their crimes have this level of Secrets, as do Anathema living in the Imperial City. Three-point secrets are deadly serious affairs. If the authorities find out, it will mean death or a comparably unpleasant fate. This level is the purview of traitors, cannibals, assassins and those who commit the most heinous and depraved acts. Quite a number of upstanding members of House Cynis hide such secrets as a result of indulging the varied excesses of their orgies. Secrets of greater value may exist, but these outrageous blasphemies are left wholly to the demented imaginations of players and Storytellers.
compatibility: Any character type, including Alchemicals; no splat-specific variant is given. The source's 'Anathema living in the Imperial City' example is Creation-specific flavor and less directly relevant to an Autochthonia-based story, but the underlying mechanic (a dangerous secret scaling 1-3 points) applies generally.
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Players Guide's universal Chapter One, "Merits and Flaws" (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json). Derived from the Players Guide's universal Chapter One (p. 37/PDF 38).

name: Disciple
summary: The character's superiors have entrusted her with a student she must train and look after, unable to abandon the relationship without permission from a higher-ranking authority; scales 1-5 points by the disciple's demands on the character's time and the consequences of the disciple's misbehavior.
mechanics: The character's superiors have entrusted her with a student that she must train and look after. In effect, the character is the mentor of her pupil, save that she cannot abandon the relationship without permission from those higher ranking than her. The student has the potential to become as powerful as the character, given time and experience. The disciples of Exalted are usually themselves Exalted, while heroic mortals typically take on other mortals as students. The value of this Flaw depends on the cooperativeness of the disciple and the level of obligation/contact required. For one point, the disciple is cooperative and requires minimal attention. The disciple may be a child whom the character tutors in poetry once a week or an eager (and blessedly harmless) acolyte hoping to become an immaculate monk. For two points, the disciple requires more regular attention, probably for several hours at a time every few days. Alternately, the character may be responsible for providing food and shelter in addition to infrequent tutelage. Three points indicates a disciple requiring daily instruction or a rebellious student seen less frequently. As the character's superiors will hold the character responsible for the rash actions of a wayward disciple, it is incumbent upon her to monitor and discipline the student. A four-point disciple lives with the character and follows her almost everywhere, intruding on virtually every facet of the character's life. It is also possible that the character sees the disciple daily, but the student is a spoiled brat or utter fool who causes regular trouble and mishap (intentionally or otherwise). A five-point disciple is a teacher's nightmare given form, an insipid, cloying wretch or a willfully malicious terror indulging in wanton mayhem for the sheer fun of it. Woe to the sorcerer suffering the pangs of a five-point disciple. Should a character fail in her teaching duties, unpleasant consequences invariably follow. The disciple may be given a worse disciple as an object lesson or may temporarily be stripped of rank (losing dots of Backing, Command, Liege or other status-based Backgrounds as appropriate). Paid tutors will lose the income gained from that tutelage. The character may even lose the respect and attention of her own disappointed mentor. The Storyteller should ensure that characters treat their disciples respectfully or suffer as befits the specifics of the assignment. It is possible to represent a useful disciple through dots of Followers or Henchmen (another Exalted is probably worth 3 to 5 dots worth of either), though usefulness in no way mitigates the obligations of the character to the student. This Flaw is particularly common among Sidereals and Immaculates, both of whom depend on a rigid hierarchy for training. Storytellers should always remember that this Trait is a Flaw, not a Merit. Without supplementary Backgrounds, disciples always create more work and trouble than any possible benefit they provide.
compatibility: Any character type, including Alchemicals; no splat-specific variant is given, though the source notes this Flaw is particularly common among Sidereals and Immaculates due to their rigid training hierarchies.
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Players Guide's universal Chapter One, "Merits and Flaws" (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json). Derived from the Players Guide's universal Chapter One (pp. 37-38/PDF 38-39). Fits an Alchemical assigned a junior member of her own Sodality or Tripartite branch to train.

name: Enemy/Rival
summary: The character has earned the enmity of an individual or group; functions as a reverse Allies Background, with a point value matching the power of the character's foes -- up to a Deathlord, First Age survivor, or Third Circle fetch at five points.
mechanics: The character has earned the enmity of an individual or group. This Flaw functions like a reverse of the Allies Background, with a corresponding point value matching the power of the character's foes. Thus, two enemies equivalent to starting characters would award two points, as would a more experienced adversary. At five points, the character might contend with the wrath of a powerful god, a Deathlord, an Exalted survivor of the First Age, a Third Circle fetich or a similarly potent being. The only difference between a rival and an enemy is that the former is a member of an organization to which the character belongs, but the underlying nature of the animosity and adversity remains the same, but neither the rival nor the character may openly act against the other without professional reprisal from their organization. Thus, a rival represents a more subtle enemy, one that cannot overcome with brute force alone.
compatibility: Any character type, including Alchemicals; the five-point tier's flavor examples are setting-color, not eligibility restrictions.
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Players Guide's universal Chapter One, "Merits and Flaws" (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json). Derived from the Players Guide's universal Chapter One (p. 37/PDF 38).

name: Wanted
summary: The character is a known criminal or has otherwise incurred the wrath of authorities willing to send hunters after her, regardless of actual guilt; scales from a minor crime like an escaped slave or defaulted loan (1 pt.) to inherent treason such as consorting with the Deathlords, fleeing rebellion, or assassinating a king (5 pts.).
mechanics: The character is a known criminal, or her actions have somehow incurred the wrath of authorities willing to send hunters after her. Whether or not she is actually innocent is irrelevant. For one point, the character is most likely an escaped slave or has defaulted on a moderate loan, committed a theft or become involved in some other minor crime involving another's property. Pursuit will be slight if at all, though the character will need to keep a low profile if she ever returns home. Three points indicates a murder or violent crime and a certainty of pursuit, most likely leading to death or lengthy imprisonment. Five points indicates the character has committed an act of inherent inexcusable treason: consorting with the Deathlords or fleeing a rebellion, assassinating the king, etc. Storytellers should use these guidelines to interpolate crimes rated at two or four points.
compatibility: Any character type, including Alchemicals; the five-point tier's flavor example ('consorting with the Deathlords') is Creation-specific setting-color for the severity of treason, not an eligibility restriction -- an Alchemical equivalent might involve betraying the Tripartite or aiding a Gremlin/Voidbringer faction.
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Players Guide's universal Chapter One, "Merits and Flaws" (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json). Derived from the Players Guide's universal Chapter One (pp. 37-38/PDF 38-39).

name: Disturbing
summary: The character makes others uncomfortable through an indefinable aura of menace (not necessarily ugliness or rudeness), adding 1 (2 pts.) or 2 (3 pts.) to the difficulty of all Social rolls not based on intimidation, and causing most people to give the character a wide berth.
mechanics: Characters with this Flaw make others uncomfortable. It's not that they are necessarily ugly or even rude, but they exude an indefinable aura of menace that discomfits those around them. For two points, this adds 1 to the difficulty of all Social rolls not based on intimidation. For three points, this penalty increases to 2. In general, characters with this Flaw can expect most people to give them a wide berth and to minimize contact even when Social rolls do not actually come into play.
compatibility: Any character type, including Alchemicals; no splat-specific restriction noted.
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Players Guide's universal Chapter One, "Merits and Flaws" (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json). Derived from the Players Guide's universal Chapter One (p. 38/PDF 39).

name: Damaged Artifact
summary: An Artifact owned through the Artifact Background has suffered damage that impairs its function, scaling from minor damage (1 pt., e.g. -1 to a weapon's damage/accuracy or armor's soak) up to near-total damage (3 pts., artifact presently useless but repairable). Points gained cannot exceed the Background/bonus points spent obtaining the artifact, minus at least one remaining point of Artifact rating.
mechanics: One of the mystical wonders owned by the character through purchase of the Artifact Background has suffered damage, either in the distant past or since it has fallen into her possession. The extent of this damage and the effect of that damage on the artifact's ability to function correctly depend on the number of points invested in this Flaw. One point indicates minor damage. A weapon may lose a point of damage or accuracy or some other characteristic, while armor loses an equivalent number of points from its lethal and bashing soak or other ratings. More complicated artifacts will function correctly most of the time or with slightly reduced function all of the time (as arbitrated by the Storyteller). Two points indicates major damage, costing five points from weapons and armor or resulting in half effectiveness or half consistency from complicated devices. Three points indicates near-total damage. The artifact is presently useless, though it may be repaired. Fixing a damaged artifact requires a proportionally complex and expensive process appropriate to the damage and the nature of the object. Repairing a shattered daiklave is considerably easier and cheaper than repairing a long-abandoned First Age warstrider. Players may not gain more points from this Flaw than the rating of Background and/or bonus points spent obtaining the artifact, whichever is less. If so desired, characters may begin play with artifacts damaged to a degree beyond the amount of points obtained through, though they receive no benefit for doing so. Characters must have at least one more point of Artifact than the points obtained with this Flaw. The Solar craftsman Velgash found tattered wings of the raptor in a tomb (see BoTC, p. 95). Using the Artifact Background available to Solars, Velgash's player had to spend four points to obtain this artifact. He may thus gain the full three points from Damaged Artifact to represent a presently useless pair of wings. If Velgash's player instead wished a bent and mangled daiklave, he could not gain more than two points from the Flaw, even if the daiklave were all-but completely ruined. However, if the Abyssal tomb robber Clutching Owl began play with the same tattered wings, he could not receive more than two points from their condition, since it would cost only two points to obtain the wings with the Abyssal version of the Artifact Background (see E:Ab, p. 131).
compatibility: Any character type with the Artifact Background, including Alchemicals. Points obtainable are capped by the Background/bonus points spent on the specific artifact; Alchemical's own altered Artifact Background (artifact-background-altered) is unusually generous (each dot buys three dots of Artifact-rated gear, and the Background may reach ***** during character creation without bonus points), so an Alchemical typically needs to spend fewer Background dots than a Solar or Abyssal to obtain an equivalent item, which correspondingly caps how many points this Flaw can yield for the same piece of gear.
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Players Guide's universal Chapter One, "Merits and Flaws" (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json). JUDGMENT CALL, FLAGGED (mirrors the source's own worked Solar-vs-Abyssal example): derived from the Players Guide's universal Chapter One (p. 38/PDF 39). Cross-checked against artifact-background-altered's more generous per-dot value for Alchemicals; a Storyteller adjudicating this Flaw for an Alchemical should compute the cap using that altered Background's costs, not the core-book Artifact Background the source example uses for Solars.

name: Debt
summary: The character owes goods or standing to an individual or organization of substantial power. This Flaw functions as an inverse of the character's Class rating (adapted from the source's inverse-Resources framing, since Alchemicals use Class instead of Resources), using the same 1-5 rating scale; failure to make scheduled payments brings hunters, militia, or worse.
mechanics: The character owes money or goods to an individual or organization of substantial power, such as a wealthy Dynast or even the Guild itself. The character must either pay regular installments with interest or promise a full repayment as of a certain date agreed upon by both parties. If the character fails to meet her obligations on schedule, unpleasant consequences will follow. The creditor will send hunters or the militia after her or worse. Wise creditors will avoid killing the character, if only to ensure they ultimately receive payment, but others may accept the loss to set an example for other debtors. This Flaw functions as an inverse of the Resources Background with an identical rating system. Thus, a character with four points of Debt owes a sum equal to Resources 4. It is possible for characters to have both Debt and Resources, provided the former exceeds the latter. Such characters must pay small installments over time, no doubt terrible interest all the while. Players who buy off Debt with Resources accumulated in play or borrowed from another lender do not need to spend experience points to do so.
compatibility: Any character type, including Alchemicals, with an adaptation: since Alchemicals have no separate Resources Background (folded into Class per class-background), this Flaw functions as an inverse of Class rather than of Resources, using the same 1-5 rating scale.
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Players Guide's universal Chapter One, "Merits and Flaws" (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json). JUDGMENT CALL: derived from the Players Guide's universal Chapter One (pp. 38-39/PDF 39-40). Adapted the inverse-Resources framing to inverse-Class, mirroring the Cache Merit's adaptation above.

name: Unbidden Oracle
summary: At least once per story but no more than once per scene, the character unintentionally speaks prophetic words of ill omen, invariably at the most inopportune moment; such prophecies almost always come true. A point of Willpower can be spent to prevent an outburst, though important prophecies will eventually find their way out.
mechanics: At least once per story, but no more than once per scene, a character with this Flaw speaks prophetic words of ill omen without meaning to. Such outbursts invariably come at the most inopportune or impolitic moment, such as to a paranoid king who believes the speaker intones a curse against him. Prophecies obtained from this Flaw almost always come true -- or would come true if the blurted warning didn't prompt countermeasures. Then, too, some prophecies fulfill themselves, and seeming flight from destiny may be the very thing that fulfills that fate. Only rarely will an unbidden oracle speak of his own impending misfortune. Players may prevent a prophetic outburst by spending a point of Willpower, but prophecies of any importance will find their way into the oracle's mouth eventually. It is usually wiser to allow fate to speak as it wills or else it chooses an even less convenient time. While they represent a rare and frightening mystery to mortals, characters with this Flaw are actually the unwitting minor tools of the Bureau of Destiny, a phenomenon to correct for dooms that come about as a result of ambient Essence disruption. Where it is imprudent or inefficient to send an agent of the bureau, a memorandum attached to the fate strand of a prophet can ensure a warning reaches the right ears at an auspicious moment.
compatibility: Any character type, including Alchemicals; no eligibility restriction. The source's Bureau of Destiny framing is Creation/Sidereal-specific lore color and does not restrict who may take the Flaw.
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Players Guide's universal Chapter One, "Merits and Flaws" (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json). Derived from the Players Guide's universal Chapter One (p. 39/PDF 40).

name: Dark Fate
summary: No matter how heroic her deeds, the character will ultimately suffer or bring about some great tragedy at its appointed time, defying even the Maidens' intervention; severity scales from a lifetime of petty miseries or a painful demise (1 pt.) to epic, empire-crumbling catastrophe (5 pts.). Celestial Exalted with this Flaw pass similar dooms to the next soul bearing their Essence; Sidereals are normally exempt unless they have betrayed their role in the Bureau of Destiny.
mechanics: No happy ending awaits a character with Dark Fate. No matter how heroic and glorious her destiny and deeds, she shall ultimately suffer or bring about some great tragedy at its appointed time, defying the most potent sorcery, astrology and divine intervention short of the Maidens themselves. The specifics of a given doom may vary widely in severity depending on the number of points invested in this Flaw. A one-point doom indicates a violent and painful demise or a lifetime of petty miseries. Two points indicates some serious criminal act or betrayal of a loved one. Death by slow torture can also befall those with such a fate. For three points, the fate usually extends to a broader scope: the ruination of a family business that has lasted for generations, the end of a dynasty or the impassioned murder of one's family. Fates worse than death usually begin at this level, such as a slow descent into madness or a fall from princely splendor into utter destitution and widespread derision. Four-point dooms indicate a cursed general's army to ignoble slaughter or shatter the prosperity of a small kingdom. True damnation is also possible, be it before the sweet whispers of Deathlords or the infernal temptations of the Demon Princes. Five-point dooms bring about epic catastrophe. Entire empires may crumble in the wake of such ruin. Directed inwardly, such ruin is absolute and final. A Solar champion may become a terrible scion and slave to the Void, a figure of such dread that his very name becomes a curse on the lips of all who utter it. Death itself often seems a kindness to those who suffer Dark Fate, as few destinies match the cruelty of the broken survivor forced to live out the rest of his days knowing the horror he has wrought or become. Those fated for ruin seldom know the curse they bear, though ill portents of varying intensity typically accompany their birth or Exaltation. Any astrologer can sense the presence of doom in the horoscope of such individuals with a single success (see Exalted, p. 251). Identifying the specifics of a Dark Fate is much harder and never certain (minimum difficulty 5). As always, the fate of the dead and Abyssals live written in the stars of the Underworld rather than the stars of Creation, and not even the Maidens can change those destinies. Ironically, those cursed with Dark Fate receive the same coincidental protection as those with Destiny (see p. 25). They will survive to meet their doom healthy and happy. As with positive destiny, players may select a particular doom with Storyteller permission or leave the curse to the Storyteller's own whim. Celestial Exalted with this Flaw often pass similar dooms on to the next souls who bear their Essence. Sidereal Exalted are normally exempt from Dark Fate on account of their position in the Bureau of Destiny. As a result, only Sidereals who have betrayed their appointed role to serve the enemies of Creation may take this Flaw. Such inauspiciousness is its own bitter harvest.
compatibility: Any character type, including Alchemicals, at the full 1-5 pt. range; the source's Sidereal exemption does not apply to Alchemicals. The source's note that Celestial Exalted pass similar dooms to the next soul bearing their Essence does not apply to Alchemicals, whose single soul is permanently bound to one construct frame rather than passing to a new incarnation on death (see alchemical-life-and-death).
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Players Guide's universal Chapter One, "Merits and Flaws" (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json). JUDGMENT CALL: derived from the Players Guide's universal Chapter One (pp. 39-40/PDF 40-41). Dropped the Celestial-reincarnation-inheritance clause as inapplicable to Alchemicals; the core mechanic (a coincidentally-protected, ultimately tragic destiny) applies unchanged, and pairs naturally with the Destiny Merit above, which explicitly leaves Alchemicals uncapped.

name: Unlucky
summary: The character suffers an endless stream of purposeless misfortune (unlike Dark Fate, this has no ultimate destiny behind it). The Storyteller gets a negative luck pool equal to points invested, spendable to force rerolls of the character's rolls (keeping the worse result) or to negatively bias games of chance; the pool refreshes at the end of every story. A character can be simultaneously Lucky and Unlucky.
mechanics: A character with this Flaw suffers an endless stream of misfortune that plagues his life. Such misfortune is not the same as a Dark Fate (see p. 39) in that it has no ultimate purpose. Chance simply dislikes the character and thwarts his enterprises. The character receives a negative luck pool equal to the points invested in the Flaw. The Storyteller may spend a point of this bad luck to force the reroll of any roll on the part of the character's player at the same difficulty and target number as the original roll. The least successful result of these applies unless the character spends additional points of bad luck to force another reroll and so on until the Storyteller runs out of luck or accepts the outcome of the lowest roll. Alternately, the Storyteller may spend points of bad luck to negatively influence a game of chance or other completely random event involving the character. Used in such fashion, the Storyteller rolls one die, subtracting one from the result for every luck point spent. If this yields a result of 5 or less, the outcome opposes the character. Strangely enough, characters may be simultaneously Lucky (see p. 27) and Unlucky. Although the two can cancel (particularly in contests of chance), the Storyteller and the player would not spend their respective luck points to affect the same rolls. A character blessed with mixed fortune experiences great highs and lows without any mediocrity, winning a king's ransom in a game and losing it the next night. Characters with this Flaw refresh their pool of bad luck at the end of every story.
compatibility: Any character type, including Alchemicals; no splat-specific restriction noted.
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Players Guide's universal Chapter One, "Merits and Flaws" (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json). Derived from the Players Guide's universal Chapter One (p. 40/PDF 41). Can stack with the Lucky Merit exactly as for other splats.

name: Beacon of Power
summary: Exalted with this Flaw cannot hide their divinity: they have only a single Essence pool (Personal + Peripheral combined), all of which counts as Peripheral for anima-display purposes, greatly increasing the risk of revealing themselves as Anathema (or, for Terrestrials, of destructive anima flux). Costs the same 4 points for all Exalt types, but Solar Night Caste and (per the same restriction) Day Caste Exalted may not take it.
mechanics: Exalted with this Flaw cannot hide their divinity. Such characters have only a single Essence pool equal to the sum of their Personal and Peripheral Essence, all of which is considered Peripheral for the purposes of anima displays. This Flaw costs the same for Exalted of all types: The dangers of revealing oneself as Anathema are balanced against the destruction wrought by Terrestrial anima flux. Night and Day Caste Exalted may not take this Flaw.
compatibility: Open to Exalted of all types, including Alchemicals, at the same flat 4-point cost. The source bars only Night and Day Caste Exalted (Solar Night Caste; Abyssal Day Caste) from taking it; no Alchemical Caste (Orichalcum, Moonsilver, Jade, Starmetal, Soulsteel) is named, so any Alchemical Caste may take this Flaw.
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Players Guide's universal Chapter One, "Merits and Flaws" (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json). Derived from the Players Guide's universal Chapter One (p. 41/PDF 42). Merges an Alchemical's Personal and Peripheral Essence pools into a single always-visible pool for Anima Banner purposes, interacting directly with alchemical-anima-banners-universal.

name: Weak Essence
summary: The character suffers stunted magical development (or recently received Exaltation), reducing starting Essence rating to 1 and severely limiting Charm selection. New Exalts may withhold up to five Charms in reserve (waiving their experience cost but not training time) until Essence can be raised in play. Other magical beings with a normal starting Essence of 2 may also take this Flaw; Dragon Kings are an exception since their Essence-1 form is a feral predator unsuitable for players.
mechanics: Individuals with this Flaw suffer stunted magical development, or perhaps they only recently received Exaltation. This circumstance reduces the character's starting Essence rating to 1, severely limiting Charm selection. If used to represent a new Exalt, the player may choose to withhold up to five Charms in reserve (typically until after the character can raise Essence in play). Withheld Charms waive their experience cost, though they still require the same training time. Other magical beings may take this Flaw, provided that they normally have a starting Essence of 2. Dragon Kings are an exception to this rule, since those with Essence 1 are feral predators unsuitable for players.
compatibility: Available to any newly-Exalted Alchemical starting at Essence 1 instead of the normal Essence 2 starting rating.
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Players Guide's universal Chapter One, "Merits and Flaws" (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json). Derived from the Players Guide's universal Chapter One (p. 41/PDF 42). An Alchemical taking this Flaw may withhold up to five installed Charms in reserve (no bonus-point/experience cost, but full Refitting/training time still required) until her Essence is raised in play via the normal Refitting process (alchemical-refitting-essence-and-evolution).

name: Ghost Cestus (Artifact •••)
summary: Universal cross-splat artifact: an armored fighting glove (cestus) enchanted with orichalcum, moonsilver, starstone, or (most commonly) jade so its punches and grapples can strike and subdue spirits, ghosts, and gods who are normally untouchable to mortal fists.
requirements: None (usable by mortals, magicians, sorcerers, or any Exalt without special training).
mechanics: Ghost cesti work against umbrood and ghosts just as well as against normal humans, requiring no special training to use. When a character fights using ghost cesti, the player makes all the normal dice rolls for unarmed combat and inflicts the normal, Strength-based damage of the combat maneuver, but instead of health levels, the character inflicts points of temporary Willpower loss on the spirit target (see Exalted core rulebook p. 147 for the total effects of Willpower loss on spirits/humans). The victim can soak this attack using her own Willpower. Spirits reduced to 0 Willpower this way become totally obedient to whoever subdued them. Spirits and mortals both recover lost Willpower from this effect as if it were bashing damage. Ghost cesti cannot outright kill a spirit -- that requires more dreadful and powerful magic -- but a cestus-wielding warrior or wizard can pummel even a powerful spirit into submission, since spirits are unused to taking uppercuts from 'mere mortals.'
compatibility: Any wielder (mortal, magician, sorcerer, or Exalt of any splat, including Alchemicals); a local spirit challenged the Empress's authority once and she sent a champion armed with ghost cesti to subdue it, and non-Exalted priests of the Immaculate Order also carry ghost cesti.
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Storyteller's Companion, Chapter Four: Further Wonders, 'Ghost Cestus (Artifact •••)', printed pp. 77-78 (PDF 78-79) (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json, recorded there as the master copy of this universal, non-splat-restricted artifact catalog). id/name/mechanics/cost/citation copied unchanged. The unarmed-combat, Strength-based, Willpower-damage mechanic has no dependency on a biological body and transfers cleanly to an Alchemical's vat-built frame; an installed Alchemical simply wears the cestus like any other piece of equipment over or in place of a hand.

name: Sling Bow of Ice (Artifact •••)
summary: Universal cross-splat artifact: a bow-and-sling hybrid weapon common in the First Age, made of mingled black and blue jade, that fires bullets or bolts which explode on impact into a cloud of snow and shivering, uncontrollable cold, freezing the ground and everyone nearby.
requirements: An Essence-manipulating wielder (the weapon itself is inert in the hands of a mortal with no Essence to fuel it).
mechanics: A sling bow resembles a normal bow, but instead of arrows it fires bullets of stone or metal, or a sling. These particular sling bows are fashioned of mingled black and blue jade carved with a fine tracery of frost ferns. A bolt of black or blue jade fired from the weapon explodes on impact into a cloud of snow and ice that sets everyone within 20 feet shivering uncontrollably, no matter how warmly they are dressed, unless they carry a bit of orichalcum or are protected by magic that shields them from cold. It also coats the ground with a thin layer of slippery ice, making it hard to remain upright. The Sling Bow requires a single mote of Essence to fuel its magic; the wielder rolls Essence + Archery. For each success, everyone within 10 feet of the impact loses one dot of Dexterity from frostbitten numbness and slipping on the icy ground; a character reduced to 0 Dexterity can do nothing but huddle in misery. A character's Essence is subtracted from the number of successes rolled. The supernatural cold lasts one turn per success rolled in mild weather, and five minutes per success if the weather is already chill. Anyone who enters the zone regains Dexterity per turn; anyone who leaves it regains Dexterity per turn. A character may soak the cold using her Essence rating; the weapon does not affect Undead at all. A person who carries a bit of orichalcum, or characters with charms or spells that protect them from extreme cold, become immune to the effect. In the First Age, soldiers operating alongside Sling Bow-armed Exalted wore orichalcum rings to protect themselves from the weapon's effect; since the art of forging orichalcum was lost centuries ago, latter-day warriors must exercise care when employing the Bow.
compatibility: Any Essence-manipulating wielder (any Exalt, sorcerer, or Essence-wielding magician, including an installed Alchemical); historically used by General Tepet Hala in the Great Eastern War, where it drove the Eastern Army across a river and let him take the enemy army by surprise.
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Storyteller's Companion, Chapter Four: Further Wonders, 'Sling Bow of Ice (Artifact •••)', printed p. 78 (PDF 79) (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json, recorded there as the master copy of this universal, non-splat-restricted artifact catalog). id/name/mechanics/cost/citation copied unchanged. The Essence + Archery roll and Dexterity-drain effect have no dependency on a biological body and transfer cleanly to an Alchemical wielder; the frostbite-style Dexterity loss is written as a generic numbing/traction effect, not a biological cold-injury effect, so it applies to a vat-built frame the same way it applies to any other wielder.

name: The Golden Viper (Artifact •••••)
summary: Universal cross-splat artifact: a First Age automaton shaped like a six-foot orichalcum-and-jewel serpent, intelligent enough to speak and advise its owner, that serves whoever possesses it and can transmute a bite victim's flesh into gold.
requirements: Ownership of the Viper following the death of its previous owner (it serves anyone who possesses it once its prior master has died).
mechanics: The Golden Viper is the most intelligent automaton known, and even First Age texts speak of it as a notable relic. This lifelike serpent, fashioned of orichalcum and jewels in a framework of starstone, stretches six feet long and is about four inches thick at its thickest. The Viper serves anyone who possesses it once its previous owner is dead. The Viper is a formidable assassin: it can move through small openings and strikes like a real serpent, coiling and lashing out. In a matter of seconds, a person bitten by the Viper turns to gold (ordinary gold, not orichalcum). Magicians and Exalted have somewhat greater resistance to the Viper's bite than do more mortal folk, but even they can be slain and transmuted. The automaton knows whatever any of its clients knew; it advises its owner on the basis of this truly awesome base of stolen knowledge and experience. The Golden Viper knows no mercy or compassion; it advises the most ruthlessly practical course whatever goal its master seeks. If the Viper's master is not already a complete cynic by human nature, she will after a few years of the Viper's callous insight into human foibles. System: Attributes: Strength 3, Stamina 5, Perception 5, Intelligence 7, Wits 5, Charisma 3, Manipulation 5, Appearance 3, Willpower 10. It lacks Virtues since these have no meaning for its cold, inhuman intellect. Instead of a list of specific Abilities, the Storyteller may assume that it has a rating of 4 in any Ability it needs, with one exception: it remembers nothing about the First Age -- or claims not to. It speaks all known languages, and rapidly learns any new one it is exposed to. Its bite inflicts a base of 6L special damage; only armor can soak this damage, though Exalted can add their Essence to their soak rating. Each health level inflicted also strips away one point of Dexterity, as the victim stiffens, and it has a soak of 7L/10B. Its health levels are -0x3/-1x2/-2x2/-4x2/Incap x3. Restoring a health level lost to the Golden Viper is a difficulty 2 task on an Intelligence + Crafts roll.
compatibility: Any owner who acquires it after its previous owner's death; functions as an autonomous intelligent servant/assassin rather than a wielded or attuned item, so it serves an Alchemical owner exactly as it would serve any other.
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Storyteller's Companion, Chapter Four: Further Wonders, 'The Golden Viper (Artifact •••••)', printed p. 78 (PDF 79) (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json, recorded there as the master copy of this universal, non-splat-restricted artifact catalog). id/name/mechanics/cost/citation copied unchanged.
