JUDGMENT CALL, FLAGGED: the Viper's bite is written as turning a victim's 'flesh' to gold, which is ambiguous for a soulless, vat-built Alchemical whose body already incorporates the Five Magical Materials rather than ordinary biological flesh. Kept selectable as an owned/serving asset (an Alchemical who acquires the Viper is served by it exactly like any other owner) since that primary use case has no flesh dependency at all; if the Viper is ever used offensively against an Alchemical target, the Storyteller should decide whether the transmutation effect (as opposed to the underlying Dexterity-draining special damage, which applies unmodified) triggers on a constructed body the same way it would on a biological one.

name: Land Ship (Artifact •••••)
summary: Universal cross-splat artifact: an extremely rare First Age vessel with a keel of interleaved yellow and black jade that lets it sail across dry land as if it were water, powered by an Essence-manipulating captain and crew.
requirements: An Essence-manipulating captain to sail it (First Age devices existed that stored Essence so a land ship could sail without an Exalted crew, but these devices have all been lost or destroyed).
mechanics: In the First Age, land ships were common. Very few of them remain -- masters of earth and water magic, working together, could craft new land ships, but this has not happened in centuries. Although land ships were once rare, war or accident has destroyed most of them; two Dragon-Blooded nobles own land ships, so does one Deathlord, and perhaps a few more await discovery. All the magic of a land ship rests in its keel -- a long, curving strip of yellow jade sandwiched between strips of black jade. The rest of the ship is ordinary wood and metal, built however the shipwright pleased, and subject to normal wear and aging. The two land ships in mortal hands are both single-masted forty-footers with high prows, one square-rigged and the other lateen-rigged; the Deathlord's ship is a 60-foot sloop. System: A land ship requires someone who can manipulate Essence to start it sailing on land, though in the First Age there were devices that contained Essence that could be used so that the vessels did not need Exalted crews. To start the vessel sailing requires one mote of Essence per hour and a simple success on an Essence + Sailing roll. With a good wind and a skilled crew, a land ship can sail 10 miles per hour, +1 mph for each success on the captain's Intelligence + Sailing roll -- wind permitting. Bad weather or obstacles such as trees or boulders result in increased difficulty. A land ship's magic has its limits: a land ship cannot sail up or down cliffs, any more than a mundane ship can sail up or down a waterfall. The one time someone tried using a land ship to breach castle walls, the ship's high prow went into the wall -- and the liquefied stone pushed the ship down into the earth. The land ship sank into the earth.
cost: 1 mote per hour of sailing (plus an Essence + Sailing roll to begin)
compatibility: Any Essence-manipulating captain (any Exalt, sorcerer, or Essence-wielding pilot, including an installed Alchemical); currently known to be owned by two Dragon-Blooded noble houses and one Deathlord.
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Storyteller's Companion, Chapter Four: Further Wonders, 'Land Ship (Artifact •••••)', printed p. 79 (PDF 80) (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json, recorded there as the master copy of this universal, non-splat-restricted artifact catalog). id/name/mechanics/cost/citation copied unchanged. Sailing on dry land via Essence + Sailing has no dependency on a biological body and transfers cleanly to an Alchemical captain; note Sail is a Rare Ability in Autochthonia before contact with Creation (see alchemical-character-creation-overview), so an Autochthonia-native Alchemical crewing one of these First Age relics may need the same weeks of unfamiliarity practice the core book already flags for living mounts/boats.

name: Singing Staff (Artifact ••••)
summary: Universal cross-splat artifact: a man-high staff of white jade, played with a rosined bow like a musical saw, that reshapes earth, sand, clay, or stone into whatever form its music evokes -- as useful for digging canals as for toppling castle walls.
requirements: An Essence-manipulating player skilled in Performance (even in the First Age, a Singing Staff required an Exalted wielder).
mechanics: The Singing Staff demonstrates the odd approach to magic taken by some First Age magicians. This man-high staff of white jade is carved in an irregular series of waves and swellings, with a knob at each end. When rubbed with a rosined bow, the Singing Staff emits a tone, like a musical saw; different parts of the staff play different pitches and timbres. If one plants the end of the Staff on the ground and plays it correctly, the land responds to the music, rising and falling like waves or shaping itself like clay molded by unseen hands. This makes the Singing Staff precious as both a tool and a weapon: the Staff's uses are limited only by the skill of its player. Singing Staves are immensely sophisticated devices, despite their simple appearance. They were never easy to make, and in the modern era are vastly more difficult -- only three are known to exist: one is in the hands of the Empress and stored among her personal effects, one is held by the Immaculates of Paisep for study, and one was lost in battle with the Tepet legions and now lies on the bottom of the Inner Sea. Although the effects of the Staves are functionally identical, each has its own musical 'tuning.' System: Wielding the Staff's magic costs one mote of Essence per turn, and even in the First Age required an Exalted wielder. Each turn of use, the Staff can reshape 100 cubic feet of earth, sand, or clay, or 20 cubic feet of stone. To use the Staff, the character's player must succeed on an Essence + Performance roll (difficulty set by the detail or magnitude of the task). The Storyteller may demand multiple rolls to succeed at lengthy tasks, or additional Ability rolls for tasks that demand specialized training. For instance, constructing an ornamental stone pavilion might require three Essence + Ability rolls to use the Staff correctly, plus another Craft roll to get the ornamental carving right.
compatibility: Any Essence-manipulating wielder with Performance skill (including an installed Alchemical); the three known Staves are held by the Empress, the Immaculate Order (for study), and one was lost when the Tepet legions were defeated and now rests at the bottom of the Inner Sea.
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Storyteller's Companion, Chapter Four: Further Wonders, 'Singing Staff (Artifact ••••)', printed pp. 79-80 (PDF 80-81) (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json, recorded there as the master copy of this universal, non-splat-restricted artifact catalog). id/name/mechanics/cost/citation copied unchanged. The Essence + Performance roll has no dependency on a biological body and transfers cleanly to an Alchemical wielder.

name: Eye of Autochthon (Artifact N/A)
summary: Universal cross-splat artifact: an immense black pearl created by the Primordial Autochthon that suppresses all physical and magical turbulence for miles around and grants its wielder god-like, Storyteller-adjudicated reality-editing power over Manses, Demesnes, and the stable lands of Creation.
requirements: None stated beyond possession; using it to perform any specific effect requires an Essence + Occult roll (see mechanics).
mechanics: The Eye of Autochthon surpasses all other magic items known, having been itself created by the Primordial Autochthon. Through the Eye, mortals can tap a tiny fraction of a power older than the world or gods or time itself -- if they dare. The Eye looks like an immense black pearl, so large that a hero might strain to wrap his arms around it. Its ebon luster draws the eye into limitless depths of dark surface, a void that could birth worlds. No force, whether natural or divine, could so much as scratch the Eye's surface, but in the First Age some unknown agency clamped the great globe into a tight-fitting nest of gimbaled rings so that the Eye could turn freely in all directions, with no need to hand-push it; nevertheless it spins by itself. System: The Eye's active powers can be summarized as a 'plot device': it can do whatever the Storyteller wants it to; in general, its history shows it can create, destroy, or usurp control of Manses and Demesnes, and can transform the stable lands of the Realm and Threshold, though it cannot transform the looser, more Essence-soaked reality of the Wyld or the shadowlands. Its passive power to suppress all disturbances of land, sea, air, and magical turbulence for a league around it operates automatically and needs no roll: no wind blows above a mild, steady breeze, no one in the area suffers Wyld contamination, charms and sorcery have normal immediate effects but any continuing effect has its duration cut in half as the Eye reorders local Essence, and magical storms, waves, and earthquakes fail or stabilize. The Eye demands great expenditure of Essence: usurping control of a Manse, for instance, might require the player to expend 15 motes for every dot of the Manse's power (how an un-Exalted prophet once used it remains a mystery). The Eye also demands great skill to use: the player must succeed at an Essence + Occult roll at +2 difficulty to discover a new use for the Eye, and roll a simple success to perform that same feat thereafter. Any botch means the character suffers some bizarre and very permanent doom -- possibly affecting everyone within a mile or so, depending on the Storyteller's mood. The Eye does not function as an instant enemy-killer: the Primordial's power does not operate on so focused a scale, and any target smaller than a castle is too puny for the Eye to affect directly.
cost: Variable (e.g. 15 motes per dot of a Manse's power to usurp it); Essence + Occult roll at +2 difficulty to learn a new use, simple success thereafter
compatibility: Any possessor, Exalted or not (an un-Exalted prophet, Ikerre, once wielded it); a Storyteller-adjudicated 'plot device' artifact rather than a routinely player-purchasable Background item -- best used as a rare, campaign-defining relic rather than a starting-character purchase.
notes: Derived from Lunar's verified transcription of the Exalted Storyteller's Companion, Chapter Four: Further Wonders, 'Eye of Autochthon (Artifact N/A)', printed p. 80 (PDF 81), the last entry in the chapter and the last mechanical content in the book (this same id/citation exists in docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/inventory/exalted-the-lunars.json, recorded there as the master copy of this universal, non-splat-restricted artifact catalog). id/name/mechanics/cost/citation copied unchanged. JUDGMENT CALL, FLAGGED: this is the one item in this batch with special thematic relevance to Alchemicals specifically, since it was 'itself created by the Primordial Autochthon' -- the very god who built the Alchemical Exalted and whose internal body, Autochthonia, is their home. The source text nonetheless writes the Eye's active powers entirely in Creation-native terms (usurping Manses and Demesnes, reshaping 'the stable lands of the Realm and Threshold'), none of which exist inside Autochthonia; kept selectable as a Storyteller-adjudicated plot-device relic, exactly as Lunar's own row frames it, but noting that an Alchemical possessor's use of its stated powers is only meaningful once a story reaches Creation (cross-referenced to building-vats-in-creation, which documents the same Autochthonia/Creation split for this family). The irony of an Autochthon-made relic being functionally inert on its own creator's body is left for a Storyteller to play up narratively rather than a mechanical restriction.

name: Cargo Preservation Spindles (Artifact • to •••, depending on size)
summary: A set of four five-sided jade-and-orichalcum-and-moonsilver spindles, one planted in each corner of a ship's hold or cabin, that wards every crate and package inside the bounded area against rot, vermin, water damage, fire, and toppling as long as the goods stay within the warded space.
requirements: None beyond owning the four-spindle set and the labor of introducing each piece of cargo to the spindles before a voyage; no Essence expenditure or roll is described.
mechanics: Cargo preservation spindles come in a set of four, ranging in size from slender spires a handbreadth high to slender pillars nearly as tall as a man; all four in a set share the same five-sided, double-pointed basic form. The shorter end of each spindle sets into a socket carved into the decking or a candlestick-like holder, with one spindle placed in each corner of the room or hold to be protected; larger spindles protect proportionally larger spaces, from a small passenger cabin up to a full cargo hold. To use the spindles, the owner must first introduce each piece of cargo to be protected by forcing the long end of a spindle into the corresponding corner of the crate (far enough to leave a mark, not far enough to damage it) while describing the crate's contents in general terms; goods radically different from that description are not protected, so a smuggler's hidden contraband is left completely unprotected even while the surrounding legitimate cargo stays pristine. Once warded, cargo is protected from nearly all damage: food will not rot, spoil, or be eaten by vermin (though food removed from its container ages normally); even the thickest brine cannot damage the goods with water; crates stay put under all but the heaviest seas and their contents remain undamaged even if a crate topples; the spindles will not stop theft, but anyone who touches a warded crate or package immediately catches fire if they have stolen anything from it. Protection only holds while the cargo remains within the hold or room bounded by the four spindles; cargo removed from that area loses protection until returned (with no retroactive penalty -- food taken out does not suddenly spoil). Each set is carefully faceted from all five types of jade bound together with bands of orichalcum and pins of moonsilver, with every facet carved with the symbol of the Elemental Dragon of Jade; the enchantment and rarity of moonsilver/orichalcum in sufficient quantity make new sets very hard to produce today, but large numbers of pre-existing sets survive, and many ships (particularly Realm vessels) carry one or more sets.
compatibility: Any owner able to place and use the four-spindle set aboard a ship or in a warded room; no Essence-manipulation requirement is stated, so mortals, magicians, and any Exalt (including an installed Alchemical) can use a set exactly the same way.
notes: Chapter Four: Creatures, Gods, Charms and Artifacts, 'Artifacts of the Waves' section opener and 'Cargo Preservation Spindles (Artifact • to •••, depending on size)', printed pp. 123-124 (PDF 124-125), the first artifact in this book's naval artifact catalog. Read from a rendered page image (this PDF has no text layer); printed page number confirmed against the visible page-footer numeral, matching the pdfPage = printedPage + 1 rule used elsewhere in this project. JUDGMENT CALL: this item has no Essence cost or roll and no dependency on a biological body, so it transfers cleanly to an Alchemical owner; it is naval/cargo-hold equipment written for Creation's seas and trade routes, which have no equivalent inside Autochthonia (no Creation-style oceans -- see manse-background-altered/building-vats-in-creation for the same Autochthonia-vs-Creation split applied elsewhere in this family's inventory), so it is kept selectable but is only meaningfully obtainable/usable once a story reaches Creation, the same reasoning already applied to Sun-Seared and Hidden Manse in this family's Players Guide rows.

name: Armor of Aquatic Puissance (Artifact ••••)
summary: First Age articulated plate armor inlaid with black jade and topped by a locking blue-jade helm, dating from before the Contagion, that lets its wearer breathe, see, swim at double speed, and move without penalty underwater for Stamina + Endurance hours at a stretch, and carries two Hearthstone sockets.
requirements: Commitment 8 motes to attune; the helm must be locked in place (a twist under the shoulder yoke) to activate the underwater-breathing effect.
mechanics: Stat block: Mobility Penalty -2/0, Fatigue Value 1, Commitment 8. Regardless of the base metal, the armor is heavily inlaid with a rare sparkling black jade; the helm is a single piece of blue jade that locks under the shoulder yoke with a twist, and the rest of the suit (excepting the faceplate) is worked in an ornate scale-and-fin pattern, with the faceplate typically carved as a bearded, angry warrior's face. All known suits date from before the Contagion and use tolerances that cannot be duplicated today. With the helm locked in place, the wearer can breathe normally in even the deepest water; the armor does not address other needs (food, etc.), so this breathing effect is limited to Stamina + Endurance hours in a row before the helm must be removed. The wearer can alter the armor's buoyancy at will, allowing quick surfacing or sinking without penalty, doubles the wearer's normal swimming rate underwater, and suffers no mobility penalties underwater (though ranged combat while wearing it is exactly as difficult underwater as it would be for an unarmored combatant). The wearer can see underwater as clearly as in air (though silt clouds, squid ink, and similar obscurants block vision just as fog or smoke would above water). The armor has sockets for two Hearthstones.
cost: Commitment 8 motes; no further activation cost once the helm is locked in place.
compatibility: Any Exalted wearer who spends significant time over or under the waves; known suits are held by the Imperial Navy, the forces of Lookshy, several aquatically inclined Dynastic houses, rumored Guild holdings, and at least two suits with the Lintha pirates; Outcastes working as pirates or merchants may own others; no Abyssal is known to own a suit, though deathknights have comparable armor of their own design.
notes: Chapter Four: Creatures, Gods, Charms and Artifacts, 'Armor of Aquatic Puissance (Artifact ••••)', printed p. 124 (PDF 125). Read from a rendered page image (this PDF has no text layer); printed page footer numeral confirmed the pdfPage = printedPage + 1 rule. JUDGMENT CALL, FLAGGED: an Alchemical wearer gets substantially reduced value from this armor's headline underwater-breathing effect, since Alchemicals already do not breathe except to speak and cannot drown at all (see alchemical-artificial-metabolism) -- the suit's Stamina + Endurance time limit on breathing simply never applies to them. The armor's other benefits (buoyancy control, doubled swim speed, no underwater mobility penalty, clear underwater vision, soak, and the two Hearthstone sockets) are unaffected by an Alchemical's construct nature and apply exactly as written. Kept selectable rather than excluded because most of its value is retained and the redundant clause is a minor efficiency loss, not an incompatibility; also flagged with the same Autochthonia-has-no-Creation-style-oceans caveat as the rest of this naval artifact set (see artifact-cargo-preservation-spindles) -- it only becomes obtainable/relevant once a story reaches Creation's seas.

name: Steelsilk Sails (Artifact ••)
summary: Rare ship's sails supposedly woven from the silk of wood spiders or spider spirits, gossamer-fine yet metal-strong, prized for speed and agility but above all for near-total durability against storms, fire, and weapons.
requirements: None stated beyond ownership and rigging the sails to a ship; the art of manufacturing new steelsilk sails has been lost.
mechanics: Steelsilk sails are supposedly made from the silk of wood spiders or spider spirits: gossamer fine and light but strong as metal, though the material is too stiff to make good armor. Whoever possesses a set typically guards it closely, keeping the sails stowed except when a ship needs its utmost speed. Sails made of steelsilk have 15B/10L soak, take 20 health levels to damage and 40 to destroy, and take only half damage from wind, waves, and fire; storms that shred ordinary silk sails, fires that turn wet canvas to ash, and weapons that cut through even reinforced canvas all fail to damage steelsilk. Repairing damaged steelsilk requires a Charm or the Crack-Mending Technique; no mundane method of mending it is known.
compatibility: Any ship owner/crew who favors speed and agility under sail and durability in battle; the art of making new steelsilk sails is lost, so existing sets are jealously guarded heirloom equipment.
notes: Chapter Four: Creatures, Gods, Charms and Artifacts, 'Steelsilk Sails (Artifact ••)', printed p. 124 (PDF 125). Read from a rendered page image (this PDF has no text layer); printed page footer numeral confirmed the pdfPage = printedPage + 1 rule. JUDGMENT CALL: this is ship's rigging with no Essence cost, roll, or dependency on a biological body, so it transfers cleanly to any Alchemical-crewed vessel; flagged with the same Autochthonia-has-no-Creation-style-oceans caveat as the rest of this naval artifact set (see artifact-cargo-preservation-spindles) -- sailing ships and their rigging are a Creation-native technology with no Autochthonian equivalent, so this is only obtainable/relevant once a story reaches Creation's seas.

name: Storm Sapphire (Artifact ••• for lesser stones or •••• for the black stones)
summary: A giant fist-sized-or-larger sapphire (green through light blue for lesser stones, black for the most powerful) that can calm a storm at sea by draining the wielding Exalted's own motes, Willpower, and health levels, with lesser stones only able to quell weaker storms and only the black stones able to face the worst hurricanes, tsunamis, and island-killer storms.
requirements: An Exalted wielder willing to power the stone with her own life force; a Perception + Occult roll (difficulty 2-5) can first gauge how severe an oncoming storm will be.
mechanics: Storm sapphires are giant sapphires, most the size of a man's fist or larger; the most powerful are black, though they come in all colors, with green (the least powerful) being the most common. They have the power to quell storms, calming sea and sky even under the worst conditions, but only by the wielding Exalted powering the sapphire with her own life force -- each use costs motes of Essence, Willpower, and health levels per the Storm Sapphire Effect Table below (these health levels cannot be soaked or reduced, though they heal normally afterward). A character can attempt to judge an oncoming storm's eventual strength with a Perception + Occult roll before committing to stop it (difficulty 2-5 depending on how fast the storm is building and whether its magical origin, if any, is known); a magically summoned or influenced storm is easier to read and cheaper to dispel (treat its severity as one level lower for cost purposes, and reduce the judgment difficulty by 2, minimum difficulty 2). Lesser stones (green through light blue) can disperse most storms up through Greater Gale but do nothing at all against anything stronger; only the darkest blue and true black stones can also disperse Hurricane through Island Killer-strength storms, at steeply rising cost, and the wielder does not learn the full life-force price until after committing to the attempt. Storm Sapphire Effect Table (Storm Strength: Blue/Green Sapphire cost -- Black Sapphire cost): Storm: 20 motes/2 Willpower/2 health levels -- 20 motes/2 Willpower/2 health levels. Greater storm: 25 motes/2 Willpower/3 health levels -- 25 motes/2 Willpower/2 health levels. Gale: 25 motes/3 Willpower/3 health levels -- 25 motes/3 Willpower/2 health levels. Greater gale: 30 motes/4 Willpower/3 health levels -- 25 motes/3 Willpower/3 health levels. Hurricane: unavailable -- 30 motes/4 Willpower/3 health levels. Greater hurricane: unavailable -- 35 motes/4 Willpower/4 health levels. Tsunami: unavailable -- 40 motes/5 Willpower/4 health levels. Greater tsunami: unavailable -- 45 motes/5 Willpower/5 health levels. Island killer: unavailable -- 50 motes/6 Willpower/6 health levels. A character who lacks sufficient motes or Willpower can, for storm-sapphire use only, convert health levels into motes or Willpower (1 health level = 10 motes of Essence or 1 Willpower), but only if she also lacks the resources to power the stone otherwise; she cannot choose to burn health levels purely to leave herself with more motes after the storm dissipates. Creating a storm sapphire requires a flawless sapphire, the blood of a Storm Mother, and a wind spirit that has never before seen a mortal, captured and used in a year-and-a-day enchantment performed aboard a ship floating in the clear waters of the uttermost West, out of sight of any land -- hence their extreme rarity.
cost: Variable per the Storm Sapphire Effect Table above (motes of Essence, Willpower, and unsoakable health levels, scaling with storm severity and stone color).
compatibility: Any Exalted wielder; highly prized and sought after by Exalted ship captains and fleet admirals. Storytellers are cautioned not to casually kill a player character who attempts to stop a major storm this way: only legendary storms are dangerous enough to kill a Terrestrial Exalt this way, and even those cannot overcome a Solar wielding a storm sapphire; draining six motes/Willpower plus six health levels is meant to be a serious cost, not an automatic death sentence, though sacrificing an NPC's life to save the party remains a valid heroic (or redemptive) story beat.
notes: Chapter Four: Creatures, Gods, Charms and Artifacts, 'Storm Sapphire (Artifact ••• for lesser stones or •••• for the black stones)' and the accompanying 'Storm Sapphire Effect Table', printed pp. 124-125 (PDF 125-126). Read from rendered page images (this PDF has no text layer), including a dedicated high-zoom crop of the effect table to confirm every cell precisely; printed page footer numerals confirmed the pdfPage = printedPage + 1 rule on both pages. JUDGMENT CALL: this artifact's function (calming Creation's seas/storms) and its creation ritual (performed on a ship in the uttermost West) are entirely Creation-native; Alchemicals can wield it exactly as any other Exalt (the drain is on the wielder's own Essence/Willpower/health, none of which depend on a biological body), but it is only obtainable/relevant once a story reaches Creation's seas, per the same Autochthonia-vs-Creation caveat applied across this naval artifact set (see artifact-cargo-preservation-spindles).

name: Cord of Winds (Artifact •)
summary: A relatively common silken cord (usually light blue) tied with up to 20 knots, each binding a minor air elemental that will serve for a day and a night raising wind on request once untied, after which it is free to depart; a knot can also be unraveled in a hurry as an extended Wits + Sail task.
requirements: None beyond owning the cord; even mortal sorcerers can produce them, and untying a knot in a hurry requires an extended Wits + Sail roll rather than any Essence expenditure.
mechanics: A relatively common artifact, produced by even mortal sorcerers, with partially-discharged examples found on many ships, even small ones, since they have been made in large numbers over the centuries. The cord is normally silken, usually light blue but possibly any color, adorned with a number of knots; each knot holds a minor air elemental bound inside it. If released, an elemental serves for a day and a night, raising wind on request, after which it is free to depart; any attempt to detain an elemental past its service will be poorly received and may well bring retribution down on the offending party at some later point. Most cords have 20 knots when first created, of different sizes and complexity: the smaller, simpler knots hold elementals that are little more than breezes, while the larger, more complex knots hold more powerful elementals. Unraveling a knot in a hurry is an extended Wits + Sail task; the difficulty depends on the power of the bound elemental -- a simple breeze's knot has difficulty 4, while the knot securing a powerful zephyr or gale might have difficulty 10, though such powerful elementals are only rarely bound into a cord of winds and most bound elementals or spirits have a permanent Essence less than 4. Any knot can also be untied given time, if one is patient enough not to simply cut it in half.
compatibility: Any owner or user, mortal or Exalted (including an installed Alchemical); no Essence expenditure is described for releasing a knot's elemental, only the extended Wits + Sail roll to unravel it quickly under pressure.
notes: Chapter Four: Creatures, Gods, Charms and Artifacts, 'Cord of Winds (Artifact •)', printed pp. 125-126 (PDF 126-127). Read from rendered page images (this PDF has no text layer), including two dedicated high-zoom crops to confirm the paragraph's exact wording where the base render's small text was harder to read; printed page footer numerals confirmed the pdfPage = printedPage + 1 rule. JUDGMENT CALL: this item has no Essence dependency and no reliance on a biological body (only a Wits + Sail roll to unravel a knot quickly), so it transfers cleanly to an Alchemical user; it is written as ship's equipment for raising wind at sea, so it carries the same lighter version of the Autochthonia-has-no-Creation-style-oceans caveat as the rest of this naval artifact set (see artifact-cargo-preservation-spindles), though a bound air elemental could plausibly also be put to use raising an air current inside an enclosed Autochthonian space at a Storyteller's discretion.

name: Wavecleaver Daiklaive (Artifact ••)
summary: An uncommon, unusually short daiklaive (rarely exceeding three feet of blade) favored by Terrestrials of House V'neef and House Peleps for shipboard work, thick-bladed and strong-edged enough to double as a tool that can hack through steel cable or chain in a single stroke, with sockets for two Hearthstones.
requirements: Minimum Strength ••; attunement as a normal daiklaive-class artifact weapon.
mechanics: Stat block: Speed +3, Accuracy +2, Damage +5L, Defense +1, Minimum Strength ••. Wavecleavers are uncommon weapons wielded mostly by Terrestrials of House V'neef and House Peleps, though most Dynastic houses have a small number of them. Perhaps the shortest daiklaives made, rarely exceeding three feet in blade length, they are well suited for work belowdecks, where cramped quarters and low ceilings are the norm. Their thick blades and strong edges make them useful as tools as well as weapons; even steel cables or chains will rarely withstand more than a single hack from a wavecleaver's curved blade. Wavecleavers typically have sockets for two Hearthstones, since Exalted who spend their careers on the water are more likely to rely on these gem-like talismans for survival.
compatibility: Any Exalted wielder meeting the Minimum Strength requirement; most common among House V'neef and House Peleps Dragon-Blooded, with small numbers held by other Dynastic houses.
notes: Chapter Four: Creatures, Gods, Charms and Artifacts, 'Wavecleaver Daiklaive (Artifact ••)', printed p. 126 (PDF 127). Read from a rendered page image (this PDF has no text layer); printed page footer numeral confirmed the pdfPage = printedPage + 1 rule. JUDGMENT CALL: a daiklaive is ordinary artifact weapon equipment with no dependency on a biological body, so it transfers cleanly to an installed Alchemical wielder; it is designed around shipboard use (short blade for belowdecks work), so it carries a lighter version of the Autochthonia-has-no-Creation-style-oceans caveat noted across this naval artifact set (see artifact-cargo-preservation-spindles) -- it remains a perfectly usable close-combat weapon anywhere, but its signature shipboard-utility framing (hacking cables/chains belowdecks) is most relevant once a story reaches Creation's seas.

name: Light Implosion Bow (Artifact ••, ••• if Hearthstone or Reagent Powered)
summary: A First Age ballista-like siege weapon, mounted on a heavy gimbaled pedestal of dark wine-red wood inlaid with the Five Magical Materials, that fires long-ranged bolts of pure Essence whose damage type and severity the Essence-channeling gunner selects per shot; typically crewed by a Dragon-Blooded, though some versions run on Hearthstones or alchemical reagents instead.
requirements: An Essence-channeling operator (any Exalt, Fair Folk, or possibly others; characters unable to channel Essence cannot operate the weapon); an unfamiliar operator's player must first succeed at an Intelligence + Lore roll at difficulty 3 to decipher the controls; keeping the weapon tuned and charged over time requires Lore •••• and Occult ••.
mechanics: These fearsome First Age relics remain beyond the full understanding of any modern savant or engineer, though operation is simple once the gunner is familiar with the controls (Intelligence + Lore, difficulty 3, to decipher them the first time). The weapon resembles a ballista mounted atop a heavy gimbaled pedestal, apparently built of dark, glossy, wine-red wood with elaborate inlays and fittings of the Five Magical Materials. Any Essence-channeling character (any Exalt type, Fair Folk, and possibly others) can fire it using Archery; it has +3 accuracy, a rate of 1, and a range of 500. Before firing, the gunner selects the damage type, and the severity scales with how many motes of Essence are channeled into the weapon: 1 mote inflicts either 7B or 5L damage (gunner's choice of setting) on everything within a 10-foot radius of the point of impact (in naval combat, this setting is used against rigging or troops); 2 motes keeps the same range and area of effect but raises the damage to 15B or 12L. Stat-table summary: Accuracy +3, Damage 7B/5L (1 mote) or 15B/12L (2 motes), Rate 1, Range 500, Naval Range Long, Naval Rate of Fire 3/turn, Minimum None, Artifact rating •• or •••. The pedestal must be mounted securely to a solid surface to fire, and the weapon has a 360-degree horizontal and 90-degree vertical (30 degrees below to 60 degrees above horizontal) arc of fire. Some versions are powered by Hearthstones and some by alchemical reagents instead of a living gunner's own Essence, though typically one is simply manned by a Dragon-Blooded who powers it personally. Keeping a Light Implosion Bow properly tuned and charged requires Lore •••• and Occult ••; maintenance parts normally cost Resources •••• per 100 firings, and the fuels/reagents used cost Resources ••• per 20 shots -- materials that are difficult, though not impossible, to find outside a large city. Archery Charms cannot be used to enhance a Light Implosion Bow's operation.
cost: 1 mote per shot (7B/5L damage) or 2 motes per shot (15B/12L damage), when powered by a living Essence-channeling gunner rather than a Hearthstone or reagent-powered version.
compatibility: Any Essence-channeling operator (any Exalt, Fair Folk, or possibly others; characters unable to channel Essence, including an unattuned mortal, cannot fire it); typically crewed by a Dragon-Blooded aboard a First Age warship, per the Artifact Ship Weapons table.
notes: Chapter Four: Creatures, Gods, Charms and Artifacts, 'Light Implosion Bow (Artifact ••, ••• if Hearthstone or Reagent Powered)', printed pp. 126-127 (PDF 127-128), plus its row in the 'Artifact Ship Weapons' stat table on printed p. 127 (PDF 128). JUDGMENT CALL: any Essence-channeling operator can fire this weapon, so it transfers cleanly to an installed Alchemical gunner with no biological-body dependency; it is written and stat-tabled as a naval siege weapon, so it carries the same Autochthonia-has-no-Creation-style-oceans caveat as the rest of this naval artifact set (see artifact-cargo-preservation-spindles), though nothing in its own mechanics actually requires a ship or open water -- it would function identically mounted on solid ground or an Autochthonian structure.

name: Lightning Ballista (Artifact ••• for a common version, •••• for a Hearthstone or elemental powered version)
summary: The primary heavy armament of larger First Age warships: a heavy brass-and-silver siege weapon, swivel-mounted centerline just aft of the prow, that fires a searing lightning blast able to instantly burn flesh/wood to ash and melt steel or stone, powered by the firer's own Essence, a bound air elemental, or a Hearthstone of Fire/Air.
requirements: An Essence-manipulating firer (it is powerless in the hands of the unExalted); Lore •••• and Occult •• to keep it properly tuned, tended, and charged over time.
mechanics: Lightning ballistae made up the primary heavy armament of larger First Age warships, with implosion bows and other weapons serving as secondary armament; though shorter-ranged than some other First Age devices, they are powerful enough to damage even the heaviest First Age hulls, and the few still in service are carefully guarded. When fired, a lightning ballista releases a blast of lightning that sears and scorches whatever it hits, instantly burning wood and flesh to ash and melting steel or stone. They are heavy, complex affairs built largely of brass and silver, requiring complex fuels and reagents in addition to the investiture of Essence to fire; typically a lightning ballista can be fueled for up to twenty firings at a time before requiring servicing and maintenance. Maintaining one requires Lore •••• and Occult ••; parts for maintenance normally cost Resources •••• every 100 firings, and the fuels/reagents used cost Resources ••• per 20 shots -- materials difficult, though not impossible, to find outside the Realm and the largest Threshold cities. Lightning ballistae are commonly mounted centerline on the hull just aft of the prow, on a swivel mount allowing the muzzle to fire on a 270-degree arc with a traverse of 45 degrees (15 down, 30 up). Only a small number of ships carried more than one, and few have survived to the present day. The most common versions were powered by the Exalted crew's own Essence (3 motes per shot); some instead used captured or willing air elementals (1 of the firer's motes plus 1 of the elemental's motes per shot); and Hearthstone-powered versions require a Hearthstone of Fire or Hearthstone of Air rated above Manse •• to provide sufficient power. All lightning ballistae are designed so that the firer must be able to manipulate Essence to activate them; they are powerless in the hands of the unExalted. Although fired using the Archery Ability, Archery Charms cannot be used to enhance a lightning ballista's operation. Lightning Ballista (elemental) +2 / 20L / 1 / 1,000 / Very Long / 3 per turn / Occult ••••, Archery • / ••••. Lightning Ballista (Hearthstone) +2 / 25L / -- / 1,000 / Very Long / 2 per turn / Occult ••, Archery • / ••••.
cost: 3 motes per shot when Essence-powered directly by the firer; 1 firer's mote + 1 elemental's mote per shot for elemental-bound versions; Hearthstone-powered versions require a Hearthstone of Fire or Air above Manse •• instead of a per-shot mote cost.
compatibility: Any Essence-manipulating firer (it is powerless in the hands of the unExalted); most commonly crewed by a Dragon-Blooded aboard a First Age warship per the Artifact Ship Weapons table, with rarer elemental-bound and Hearthstone-powered variants.
notes: Chapter Four: Creatures, Gods, Charms and Artifacts, 'Lightning Ballista (Artifact ••• for a common version, •••• for a Hearthstone or elemental powered version)', printed p. 127 (PDF 128), plus the 'Artifact Ship Weapons' stat table on the same page, the last content page of the book before the back cover (PDF 129).
